title: Safe administration, checks, records and calculations
blurb: Carry out the RPS/RCN checks before every dose, calculate safely, record what was given, withheld or refused, and support self-administration.
question: At the 08:00 round, a patient with capacity refuses her prescribed ramipril because it makes her dizzy. What should the nurse record and do?

teach.h: The professional standard for giving medicines
teach.body: The NMC withdrew its own Standards for medicines management. The RPS and RCN Professional guidance on the administration of medicines in healthcare settings (January 2019) now sets the principles across the UK, alongside your organisation's policy and Code standard 18. The registered professional who administers, or delegates administration, is accountable for their actions, non-actions and omissions. In everyday terms: you own every dose you give, and every dose you do not give.

head: Check
What you are confirming
rows: Right person, e.g. wristband and verbal confirmation
Lawful, unambiguous: name, form or route, strength, dose
Issues around consent have been considered
No known reaction to this medicine or class
Timing, frequency, route, start and finish dates
Double-checked by a second person where practicable
By anyone else, including the patient or carers
teach.caption: Ambiguities or concerns are raised with the prescriber or a pharmacy professional without delay.

steps.label: Write the formula
steps.sub: what you want / what you have x volume

teach.caption: Example: 7.5 mg prescribed, ampoule 10 mg in 2 mL: 7.5 / 10 x 2 = 1.5 mL.

teach.body: Records are kept of all medicines administered, withheld or declined, completed at the time or as soon as possible afterwards, and clear, legible and auditable. If a dose is not given, record the reason where known and notify the prescriber or team where appropriate. NICE SC1 adds two practical rules for care homes that apply everywhere: record a dose only after it has been taken, and correct errors with a single line, signature, date and time, never with correction fluid.

root.label: Risk assessment
root.sub: risks, ability, consent; repeat as needed

children.label: Level 2
children.sub: staff store; patient self-administers under supervision

teach.caption: Record the assessment, the outcome and the date and time the patient agreed to take responsibility.

teach.body: Transcribing is copying previously prescribed details so a medicine can be given, for example onto a care home chart. It is allowed only under an organisational policy, by trained and competent staff, with an audit trail. It can never add a new medicine or change a prescription. Details that are illegible, unclear, ambiguous or incomplete are not transcribed, and special care is taken with insulin, anticoagulants, cytotoxics and controlled drugs.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Kofi and Mrs Pearl
teach.body: At 08:00 Mrs Pearl, 81, who has capacity, refuses her ramipril because it makes her dizzy. Kofi respects her decision, records 'declined' with her reason on the chart, checks her lying and standing blood pressure, and informs the prescriber so the medicine can be reviewed. He does not hide it in her food, pressure her or record it as given. On admission yesterday, her medicines were reconciled within 24 hours, so the team already knows her full list.

items.label: to correct an error, signed and dated

teach.text: Do not confuse 'withheld' with 'declined'. Withheld means the nurse decided not to give it (for example, a low pulse before digoxin or nil by mouth); declined means the person refused. Both are recorded with the reason, and the prescriber is told where appropriate.

items: RPS/RCN 2019 replaced the NMC medicines standards; you are accountable for what you give and omit.
Check identity, prescription, consent, allergies, directions, calculation, medicine and expiry, storage, not already given.
Calculations are double-checked by a second person where practicable.
Record given, withheld or declined at the time, with reasons; correct errors with a single line.
Self-administration follows a recorded risk assessment; transcribing never adds or changes a medicine.

summary: You can now complete every RPS/RCN check before giving a medicine and calculate a dose safely with an independent second check. You can also record given, withheld and declined doses correctly, transcribe within policy and assess for self-administration.

A.q: Hassan, 54, is prescribed 7.5 mg of an intramuscular medicine. The ampoule contains 10 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up, and what should happen next?
options: 1.5 mL, then ask a colleague to check the calculation independently
0.75 mL, then give it straight away as the maths is simple
2.5 mL, then ask the patient to confirm the dose
1.5 mL, then give it and ask a colleague to countersign it afterwards
A.why: 7.5 / 10 x 2 = 1.5 mL. RPS/RCN 15 states calculations are double-checked by a second person where practicable, before administration.

whyNot.1: 0.75 mL comes from forgetting to multiply by the 2 mL volume.
whyNot.2: 2.5 mL would deliver 12.5 mg, more than the 7.5 mg prescribed, and a patient cannot verify a calculation.
whyNot.3: The volume is right, but a check after giving the dose cannot prevent an error.

A.q: Before giving the first dose of oral amoxicillin to Stanley, 67, the nurse sees he is wearing a red allergy wristband labelled 'penicillin'. The allergy is not recorded on the chart. What should she do?
options: Give it, as the medicines chart itself shows no recorded allergy
Give half the dose and observe him closely for a reaction
Withhold it, clarify the allergy and contact the prescriber
Give it together with an oral antihistamine as a precaution
A.why: Checking allergies and previous reactions is a required check (RPS/RCN 15). Amoxicillin is a penicillin; the dose is withheld, the allergy clarified and documented, and the prescriber contacted.

whyNot.0: The wristband is evidence of a possible allergy that must be resolved before giving it.
whyNot.1: Reducing the dose does not remove the risk of an allergic reaction.
whyNot.3: Antihistamine cover is not a safe way to give a medicine to which the person may be allergic.

A.q: At the 08:00 round, Pearl, 81, refuses her ramipril saying it makes her dizzy. She has capacity. What should the nurse do?
options: Record it as given, as she took it yesterday
Crush it into her yoghurt so she gets the dose
Leave it on her table so she can take it later if she changes her mind
Record 'declined' with her reason and inform the prescriber
A.why: Records are kept of medicines declined, with the reason, and the prescriber is notified where appropriate (RPS/RCN 17). A person with capacity has the right to refuse.

whyNot.0: Recording a dose as given when it was not is a falsified record.
whyNot.1: Hiding medicine from a person with capacity is covert administration without lawful basis.
whyNot.2: Leaving medicines unattended is unsafe, and the refusal still needs recording.

B.q: Agnes, 70, admitted for a planned hip replacement, asks to keep her own inhalers and eye drops in her locker and use them herself, as at home. What should the nurse do?
options: Complete a self-administration risk assessment and record it
Refuse, as all medicines must be kept in the ward trolley
Allow it without any assessment, as these are her own medicines
Ask her family to bring in and give her the medicines
B.why: Patients keep responsibility for some or all of their medicines unless a risk assessment indicates otherwise; the assessment and outcome are recorded (RPS/RCN 3-5).

whyNot.1: Organisations should have a self-administration policy; refusal without assessment ignores it.
whyNot.2: A risk assessment is required, covering risks, her ability and consent.
whyNot.3: Family administration does not replace a recorded assessment and secure storage.

B.q: Clive, 76, has moved from hospital to a nursing home. The nurse is transcribing his discharge medicines onto the home's chart. The insulin dose on the discharge letter is illegible. What should she do?
options: Enter the dose she thinks it most likely is
Leave the insulin off and tell the GP at the next visit
Copy yesterday's dose from his hospital blood glucose monitoring chart
Contact the prescriber to clarify the dose before transcribing
B.why: Medicines are not transcribed where details are illegible, unclear, ambiguous or incomplete, with particular care for high-risk medicines such as insulin (RPS/RCN 31).

whyNot.0: Guessing a high-risk dose risks serious harm.
whyNot.1: Omitting insulin until the next visit risks hyperglycaemia; clarification is needed now.
whyNot.2: A glucose chart is not a prescription and cannot confirm the intended dose.

B.q: During the breakfast round, Norma, 85, says she would like her tablets after eating and asks the nurse to leave them on her table. When should the nurse sign the chart?
options: Now, as the tablets have been dispensed to her
After she has been seen to take them
At the end of the round, to save time
When the next nurse takes over at handover
B.why: NICE SC1: record administration only after the dose has been taken. The nurse returns after breakfast, gives the tablets and records them.

whyNot.0: Dispensing is not administration; she may not take them.
whyNot.2: Records should be made at the time of administration, not batched.
whyNot.3: Delaying the record to handover risks missed or duplicated doses.

C.q: Frank, 63, is prescribed oral morphine solution 2.5-5 mg as required every 2 hours. He had 2.5 mg 4 hours ago with little effect and now rates his pain 8/10. Observations are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give 2.5 mg again, as that was the last dose he was given
Wait until the 6-hourly review before giving more
Give 7.5 mg, as the last dose was not effective
Give 5 mg, the top of the prescribed range, and reassess
C.why: The prescription permits up to 5 mg two-hourly; the previous dose was ineffective and it is over 2 hours since. Giving within the prescribed range, then reassessing and recording, is correct.

whyNot.0: Repeating an ineffective dose when the range allows more leaves pain undertreated.
whyNot.1: The prescription allows a dose every 2 hours; delaying leaves severe pain untreated.
whyNot.2: 7.5 mg exceeds the prescribed maximum single dose.

C.q: A student nurse finds an error she made on a medicines chart and plans to cover it with correction fluid before rewriting. What should the nurse mentor advise?
options: Strike through with a single line, then sign, date and time it
Use correction fluid, then initial the change
Tear out the page and rewrite the whole chart
Overwrite the error firmly so that the new entry is clear to read
C.why: Errors are corrected with a single line, signature, date and time, so the original remains readable and auditable; correction fluid is not used (NICE SC1).

whyNot.1: Correction fluid hides the original entry and breaks the audit trail.
whyNot.2: Destroying records removes the audit trail.
whyNot.3: Overwriting makes both entries unclear and is not auditable.

C.q: Mrs Okoro, 74, is admitted to a medical ward with her own medicines in a bag and a list from her GP. When should medicines reconciliation be completed?
options: Within 72 hours, at the time of the first consultant review
Within 24 hours, or sooner if clinically necessary
Before discharge, so the GP letter is accurate
Within 1 week, when her condition has settled
C.why: NICE NG5 1.3.1: in an acute setting, list all medicines (prescribed, over-the-counter and complementary) and carry out reconciliation within 24 hours, or sooner if clinically necessary.

whyNot.0: 72 hours is too late and risks omitted or duplicated doses.
whyNot.2: Reconciliation at admission prevents errors during the stay, not just at discharge.
whyNot.3: A week is far beyond the 24-hour standard.

reteach.title: Pause before every dose
reteach.question: If someone stopped you at the bedside and asked 'how do you know this is right?', what would you show them?

blocks.h: Prove it before you give it
blocks.body: You should be able to show: this is the right person (ID), there is a lawful and clear direction (chart), they agree (consent), they are not allergic, it is due now by this route, my sum has been checked, this is the right medicine and in date, it was stored properly, and nobody has already given it. Then you sign, at the time, for what actually happened.

blocks.text: The 'rights' are a memory aid, not the standard. The RPS/RCN checks also include consent, allergies, calculations, expiry, storage and whether the dose has already been given.

explain.body: Identity; lawful, unambiguous direction; consent; allergies; directions; calculations double-checked; medicine identity and expiry; storage; not already given.

test.q: Which check is part of the RPS/RCN pre-administration checks?
options: That the patient's relatives agree
That the medicine is on the ward formulary
That the pharmacy has a backup supply
That the dose has not already been given
test.why: RPS/RCN 15 includes checking that the dose has not already been administered by someone else, including the patient or carers.

whyNot.0: Consent is the patient's, not the relatives', unless they have legal authority.
whyNot.1: Formulary status is a prescribing issue, not a pre-administration check.
whyNot.2: Pharmacy stock is not an administration check.

explain.body: What you want / what you have x volume. Convert units first, sense-check, then a second person checks independently where practicable.

test.q: Paracetamol 250 mg is prescribed. The stock suspension is 500 mg in 5 mL. What volume is given?
options: 2 mL
2.5 mL
5 mL

whyNot.2: 5 mL would give 500 mg, double the dose.
whyNot.3: 12.5 mL would give 1,250 mg, five times the dose.

explain.body: Given, withheld or declined, at the time or as soon as possible, legible and auditable, with reasons and prescriber informed where appropriate. Record only after the dose is taken.

test.q: A nurse withholds digoxin because Mr Vale's apical pulse is 48. What must she do?
options: Record it as withheld with the reason and tell the prescriber
Leave the chart blank so that the next nurse on duty can give it later
Record it as declined by the patient
Give half the dose and record that
test.why: Withheld doses are recorded with the reason, and the prescriber is notified where appropriate (RPS/RCN 17.2).

whyNot.1: A blank entry invites a missed or duplicated dose.
whyNot.2: He did not refuse; recording 'declined' is inaccurate.
whyNot.3: Altering a dose without a prescription is not permitted.

explain.body: Self-administration after a recorded risk assessment at one of three levels. Transcribing only under policy, by competent staff, with an audit trail, never to add or change a medicine.

test.q: What can transcribing be used for, according to RPS/RCN guidance?
options: Adding a new medicine that the nurse thinks the patient needs
Changing a dose after a phone call with the GP
Copying existing prescribed details to enable administration
Converting a verbal order into a prescription
test.why: Transcribing is copying previously prescribed details to enable administration; it cannot add new medicines or alter prescriptions (RPS/RCN 24, 27).

whyNot.0: Adding a medicine is prescribing, not transcribing.
whyNot.1: Changing a dose alters the prescription, which transcribing cannot do.
whyNot.3: Only the prescriber can confirm a verbal order in writing.
